## 1. Problem Statement

- **The question:** Compare three Review Panel efforts and recommend one unified central Review Panel design. E1 is this session's reflect Tier 2 panel kernel, shadow mode and model-combination experiment on branch `ironbelly/shadow-runs`. E2 is the other session's tasklist review-panel evaluation study on `origin/ironbelly/eval-tasklist-review-panel` at commit 4a22d74213f93837d00c2c314075dd967b9a98e3 only. E3 is the #346 review-loop infrastructure on master: findings-v1, the ledger, the `superclaude review` merge/ledger/panel/telemetry CLI, the spec-panel Review Loop and the installed-only experiment variants. The one design must serve `sc:reflect` (Tier 2 shadow, then panel), `sc:workflow` tasklist review, spec review for `sc:brainstorm` and `sc:design`, and later PR code review and replacement of rf-qa style agents (BR GOAL and WHY).
- **Why it matters:** The research shows the three efforts each hold part of the answer and none holds all of it, and today neither kernel is reached by the consumers the owner wants served.
  - Reviewer identity lives in three places (reflect rotation table, the `T2Model0N` environment pool, the panel tier file), finding shape in two (reflect cards, findings-v1), merge in two (`/sc:adversarial`, `merge_round`) per the E1 requirements document (S04 §0.1, MR:105; doc-sourced), and a code-driven third merge path exists in `ensemble.py` (R13 §1, §8).
  - The #346 merge/ledger CLI has exactly one in-repo caller (one paragraph of the rules prompts file read by `/sc:spec-panel --mode critique`), and the E1 kernel is reached only by reflect's shadow steps, which no consumer turns on (R09 §7 [CODE-VERIFIED]). `sc:workflow`, `sc:tasklist`, `sc:brainstorm` and `sc:design` reach neither (R09 summary).
  - Each effort measured a different third of a run: E1 state and hashes, E2 served identity and per-attempt cost plus blind scoring, E3 a full telemetry schema that nothing writes (R08 §11).
  - E2 measured a ceiling of about 1.6 to 2.5 of 14 known defects per panel and 49 blocking findings lost at merge by length limits, so the shared parser and merge have measured defects that any unified core would inherit (S00 §0, §2.4; R02 §4 [CODE-VERIFIED against committed audit outputs]).
  - E1's Stage 2 shadow exit currently FAILS (13 of 20 runs counted, exit 1; command `uv run python scripts/reflect_shadow_exit.py`, default arguments, run 2026-11-14 at HEAD 792cf8c52, which prints `OVERALL: FAIL (shadow runs 13 of 20)`; every Stage 2 figure in this report comes from that invocation), and every failure is a contract-writing or file-placement mistake, not a quality result (R07 §10 Q7, R11 §8).
  - The experiment variants carry no valid-success verdict (R02 §8, R11 §11).
  - Open gaps are large: 94 open rows, none Critical, 30 Important (GQ §5). Scale: that is the gap-log rating; Section 4 re-rates 15 rows Critical, which are 11 distinct gaps plus 4 restatement rows: 7 distinct gaps because control C8 treats an unwired in-scope capability as Critical, and 4 (D1, D3, D4, ENS-2) on impact (see Section 4.1 row 15).
- **Trigger:** The owner asked for ALL value from both sessions and master to be captured, overlap evaluated and de-duplicated, conflicts resolved, and future use cases (PR code review, rf-qa replacement) not hindered by the final shape. The efforts overlap on the finding contract, panel resolution, clustering, merge, calibration, run recording and evaluation, and they conflict on several choices (single-reviewer veto versus debate and calibration; strict distinctness versus replicated same-model panels; observed versus pinned identity; reject versus truncate for over-length findings). On 2026-11-13 the owner changed the scope: this task produces the REPORT ONLY, with no `/sc:workflow` and no roadmap. The report will later be merged with the other session's second tech-research report through `/sc:adversarial --compare --merge`, and only then will a roadmap be built; Section 8 of the report is therefore a value-capture and migration plan, including the git constraint that `feat/review-panel` and `feat/review-panel/<name>` cannot both exist (BR WHY). E2 input is taken at commit 4a22d74213f93837d00c2c314075dd967b9a98e3 only, and differences against the other session's second report are expected and resolved in that merge (GQ O-6).

### 2.1 E1: reflect Tier 2 panel kernel and shadow mode

**What E1 is.** The reflect Tier 2 panel kernel is a set of dormant, telemetry-only review tools plus a ten-step shadow recipe in the reflect skill. The kernel code is already on `origin/master` (commit d2d8a2d16, #519, Stage 0-2 of the Tier 2 review panel); the branch `ironbelly/shadow-runs` is three commits ahead (9874d63fb, c2e3347d3, 792cf8c52), and the two skill-fix commits touch only four files: `SKILL.md` (inside §4.3a shadow steps 2, 4, 7, 10 and the §9.2 `findings_block_compliance_rate` comment), `refs/reviewer-spec.md` (the shadow instruction line :39) and two tests (S03 baseline note and §1.1 [CODE-VERIFIED via `git diff`]; S02 header). The kernel is therefore master code that E1 authored, not branch-only code.

**How it works: the authoritative legacy path (default, `--t2-engine legacy`).** The orchestrator composes two or three `reflect-reviewer` agents by model-class rotation and persona (analyzer, qa, refactorer or architect), writes three-section briefs, dispatches, persists cards, runs one blind `confidence-calibrator` per card (one card-level number), then merges by `sc-adversarial-protocol` Mode A (`--depth standard`, convergence score routing PASS at 0.75 or more, PARTIAL at 0.60 or more), runs the `evidence-validator` gate, and writes the 1.8.0 `return-contract.yaml` (S03 §2.2; R07 §1). The skill-path contract has no code writer; the orchestrator writes it (R13 §4 [CODE-VERIFIED by absence], resolving R08 gap 5). The wrapper degrades any Tier 2 run whose convergence score is below 0.80 or null and halts on any regression or drift count above zero (`contract.py:317-326`, `:377-381`; R07 §8, R05 §1).

**How it works: shadow mode (`--t2-engine shadow`, UC-1 pre only; accepted and ignored for UC-2).** Shadow runs next to the legacy steps and changes no verdict, no stable field and no `merge_method`; all panel files go under `<output>/panel/` and all fields under `telemetry:` (S03 §2.3). The ten steps are: resolve and freeze (`review panel resolve --template @reflect-pre ... --strict-distinct`, then `review manifest init`), parity check, briefs plus one findings-v2 instruction line (`reviewer-spec.md:39`), normalise with a bounded re-ask, per-finding calibration line, `review cluster` plus `review verify-citations`, the legacy debate then a written `adversarial/merged-verdict.yaml`, a kept-ids cluster pass after the evidence validator, an identity check, publish (S03 §2.3, SKILL.md :338-349). Shadow is a prose recipe the orchestrator follows; `cli/reflect/` holds no shadow code (R07 §10; S04 §0.8 doc-sourced, spot-checked by R07).

**Identity and dispatch (dated 2026-11-12 and 2026-11-13).** The panel record pins models; it does not observe them. Spike S-ID (3 probes, 2026-11-12) found self-report matched the pin 0 of 3 times and transcript `message.model` honoured 2 of 3 pins: a `haiku` pin ran `gpt-6.1-sol` because the gateway tier2 alias has no Anthropic model first; the Agent tool result does not expose the served model, only the sidechain transcript on disk does (S04 §0.7). `identity_source: observed` has no implementation (R04 G2 [CODE-CONTRADICTED as an implemented feature]); the `model_observed:` card line is consumed by nothing (R04 G3); the only served-model extraction is the offline `extract.py:42-79` of the combination study (R08 §10). A missing class collapsed a whole panel to Sonnet in the combination runs (R04 summary). The `gateway` environment has `launch: {}`, so every reflect template fails to resolve there, and `anthropic-only` is not anthropic-only at serving time (R04 summary; GQ O-2).

**The 5x3 model-combination experiment (runs 2026-11-13).** Five combinations by three repeats under `.dev/eval-workspaces/shadow-model-combos/` (`PLAN.md`, `FINDINGS.md`, `results.md`, `combos.json`, `analysis/extract.py` 193 lines). It yields leads (orchestrator speed, confidence shift, compliance) at n=3 and no quality answer: blind ground-truth scoring was not approved or run. Combo A's orchestrator was served by GLM 5.3 and Qwen3.8-max, the same models the E2 study banned, which is a likely driver of its leads; `combos.json` `status: "designed, not run"` is stale because all 15 runs exist (R11 §9, §12 gaps). The untracked `runs/pre-TASK-WF-designSpec-20261107-075614-comboC-r3/artifacts/base-e8db2fe6/` folder is an orchestrator-made base-commit archive, not a reviewer escaping its snapshot, and makes run C3 protocol-different (R11 §10 summary). Per-run cost and served identity exist only in `extract.py`, derived from the outer session log, never in the product record (R08 §10).

**Defects and constraints found.** Contract 1.8.0 is frozen: any new `merge_method` value or new top-level key fails `panel_lint` and needs a version bump, so the shared core can own resolution, cards, clustering, citation checks, calibration coverage and manifests (all telemetry) but not the merge decision or contract writer without a bump (R07 summary). EV-1 is self-attested: the verdict file it reads is written by the same orchestrator (R07 gap, GQ G-13). The calibrator agent implements a 6-dimension troubleshoot rubric with a gated-minimum formula and reflect passes no `rubric_path`, so the claim "re-grades per the 5-dim reflection rubric" is [CODE-CONTRADICTED] (R05 §4.1). Drift halts at any severity (`contract.py:380-381`) while findings-v2 forbids MINOR blocking (`findings_v2.py:107-108`) (R05 §13). `unauthorized_deviation_present` has no producer rule anywhere in the skill (R05 gap, GQ G-03). Pins C1, C6 and C14 compare against `HEAD`, so they guard only uncommitted edits (R07 §10 Q5, R12 §6).

**Evidence:** R01 §2-3; R03 §2-3; R04 §2, §4, §6-7; R05 §1, §4-5, §13; R07 §1-3, §8-10; R08 §1, §9-10; R11 §7-10, §12; S02 §1, §3; S03 §1-2; S04 §0.2-0.8; GQ C-02, C-05, G-03, G-13; `src/superclaude/cli/review/{findings_v2,card_convert,cluster,cluster_cmd,verify_cmd,manifest,manifest_cmd,panel}.py`, `src/superclaude/cli/reflect/{contract,panel_lint}.py`, `scripts/reflect_shadow_exit.py` (line numbers as given in the table rows above).

### 2.2 E2: tasklist review-panel evaluation study (commit 4a22d742)

**What E2 is.** An evaluation harness and a measured study, not product code. The hand-off states the branch changes no product code (`git diff origin/master...HEAD -- src tests` empty; doc-sourced, S00 §0) and the inventory of the commit lists only study files under `.dev/eval-workspaces/tasklist-review-panel/` (S01 §1; R09 gap 12). The study scored 106 panel runs (rows; 62 distinct reviewer-model sets, including 3 pilot arms and 30 pre-source rows), of which 71 are valid-era rows (213 row-packages, 665 individual reviewer runs; "reviewer run" means one reviewer in one row and is used only for that unit below) against 3 plan packages with 16 known defects taken from real `/sc:implement` failures: `TASK-WF-designSpec-20261107-075614` (10 known, 5 blocking in implement), `TASK-WF-makeTheAliasOnly-20261105-051649` (4 known, 3 blocking) and the control `TASK-WF-design-20261108-041415` (2 known, 0 blocking) (S00 §2.1; R11 §4). It reviews tasklist first reviews only: one round, no reviser, no re-review (S00 §2.7).

**Model-by-role observations (dated, one gateway).** `claude-sonnet-5-5` never had findings dropped at merge (446 of 446 kept) and read `source.md` in 62 of 63 runs (`gpt-6.1-terra` and `gpt-6.1-sol` also lost none, 103 of 103 and 8 of 8 kept, and opened `source.md` in 44 of 44 and 3 of 3 runs, but their reviews are empty or incomplete; `audit-D/summary.md:18`, `COMBO-REPORT.md:373`); `gpt-6-luna` is fast and thin with the weakest anchor fidelity (91.4% verbatim, 30 findings lost at merge); `muse-ember-1.0` is cheap, with 33 findings lost (the per-model counts include all dropped findings, not only blocking ones, S01 summary correction (d)); `gpt-6.1-terra` and `gpt-6.1-sol` return empty or incomplete reviews; `glm-5.3` was slow in the pilot (805-1435 s per review, `combos/SPEC.md:5`) and the owner removed it from batch 4 onward for delays (`combos/SPEC.md:98`), so no source-era glm data exists (the "adds nothing" and "800-1800 s" wording sits in `COMBO-REPORT.md` lines the file declares superseded and is not carried); `Qwen3.8-max` timed out 3 of 3 slots and was excluded by the owner yet is still listed in the packaged `tier2` (4th of 6), `tier2b` (3rd of 4) and `tier3` (2nd of 2) lists (S00 §2.3; R04 §8; order read from `review-tiers.default.json` at HEAD 792cf8c52; a gateway `live7` resolution can draw it into two slots, D11).

**Strategies that worked and failed (doc-sourced lessons).** Worked: blind scoring with an independent re-judge of 12 rows (12 of 12 agreement); ground truth from real implement failures with a `blocking_in_implement` flag; six read-only integrity audits after the data was in; replicates before any claim; an observed-model check on every run with quarantine instead of deletion; `NOFALLBACK=1` for evaluation runs; counting by agents and by a direct script (S00 §3). Failed: single-run claims, per-reviewer attribution of merged rows, treating judge-blocking as real blocking, many concurrent gateway workers (model-identity bleed), a cyclic fallback ladder that hid wrong-model runs, not shipping `source.md` from the start (S00 §3).

**Defects in the E2 harness itself (code-verified in R11, R08).** `expected_model` is overwritten on fallback (`run-reviewer.sh:58` with `:76`) and `final-table.py:44` groups panels by it; the cost glob also sums stale attempt files (`run-reviewer.sh:87`); `BLOCK_OK` greps the fence only, so invalid lines are invisible to the runner (:57); Bash is not denied under `bypassPermissions` (:48); the judge is blind to reviewer ids but not to panel name (`judge-one.sh:21`); a judge that exits 0 without `score.json` is silently dropped (`final-table.py:48`); the audit filter silently disappears when `/tmp/audit-*/flags.tsv` is missing (`final-table.py:24`); `three-way.py:4` executes a `/tmp` copy of `final-table.py`; audits A and D read attempt transcripts that are not committed (1.48 GB left out by owner order) and hard-code another worktree's paths, so they cannot be re-run from the commit (R11 §1-3; R08 §8, §12). The study bypassed `superclaude review panel resolve` (raw model ids, bash ladder), while its own `resolution-*.json` inputs show Qwen3.8-max and glm-5.3 twice in one `@live7` panel, so the hand-off claim that D11 was "not observed in the eval" is [CODE-CONTRADICTED] in data (R11 §4, R04 summary).

**Product-code defects E2 reported.** D1 to D16 against the shared review package are summarised with their current-code status in section 2.4 (S02 §5, S00 §2.4). All 16 hand-off defects that touch the package were confirmed at current code, with line numbers for D7, D11 and D12 moved (D11 now `panel.py:536-543`, D12 `panel.py:485-494`, D7 `telemetry.py:23` and `findings.py:29`) (S02 §5, R04 §10 stale docs, R03 stale docs).

### 2.3 E3: #346 review loop and installed-only experiment variants

**What E3 is.** The #346 review loop on master: a prose loop in `/sc:spec-panel` plus a deterministic CLI core. It landed through 9163bd1c7 (merge of 346Claude-integration, #498), 5d9a0ae70 (#479, P4 extension) and 77e0a7029 (#478, severity by consequence) (S05 baseline fact). It is the only place on master where a panel actually runs a verdict, and it is reached by exactly one consumer, `/sc:spec-panel --mode critique` (R09 §7).

**Master components (in `src/`).**

| Component | File (lines) | What it does | Evidence |

**How the loop runs (master).** (1) the coordinator runs `superclaude review panel resolve --run-id <loop> --kind first|re-review` (default: a panel for a first review, one reviewer for a re-review; every packaged template has `apply_to: ["first"]`, so a re-review always resolves only the fixed anchor `t1b-1`, `panel.py:600-605`); (2) each reviewer in a fresh context gets the same brief and ends with a `## Findings block` of `findings-v1` JSON lines; (3) `superclaude review merge` parses, annotates, clusters and merges the round ("also for a single reviewer"); (4) the ledger updates rows; (5) a reviser addresses the blocking ids and ends with a `fixmap-v1` block; (6) `review ledger revise --old --new --fixmap` moves touched rows to `resolved_check`; (7) stop rule: at most two fix cycles, three reviews; (8) fallback when `superclaude` is not installed: run one reviewer and say so. Master re-finds every round from full findings blocks; verify-only does not exist on master (S05 §2 [CODE-VERIFIED]; R09 §2, §7; R04 §9).

**Ledger behaviour confirmed at current lines (R02 §1.4).** D2: the clearing loop (`ledger.py:254-258`) turns every `resolved_check` row nobody re-reported into `resolved` and never reads `block_ok`; the docstring at :112 ("skipped for clearing") is [CODE-CONTRADICTED] by the code and `test_review_ledger.py:385` pins the code. D3: the merge raises only when no reviewer has a valid block (:150-157), so a round can PASS on one valid reviewer. D4: one reviewer's `blocking` flag decides a row (:187, :213-218) and one non-blocking re-report can un-block a row; `confidence` (overlap or single) is printed in the merged report but read by no decision. D16: round 4 is accepted, `--cap` is silently ignored on an existing ledger, and the round help text still says "1, 2 or 3". Per-reviewer entries store only `block_ok` and one first-error warning, so rejected line ids are never persisted (:130-134, :141-149).

**Installed-only experiment variants.** They exist in `~/.claude/` and as builds in `.dev/experiments/346-validation/phase5/final-bundle/builds/`; they are not in `src/` and not in the project `.claude/`. The hand-off statement that they exist only in the bundle is [CODE-CONTRADICTED] for this machine (S05 §1A, R09 §7).

| Variant | Installed location (lines) | Verified properties | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| ledger (find once, verify-only) | `~/.claude/commands/sc/spec-panel-ledger.md` (475); `~/.claude/skills/sc-review-ledger/` (`SKILL.md` 118, `scripts/review_ledger.py` 2668) | script is the only writer; find once at review 1, answers-only at reviews 2-3 with an evidence quote that must occur in the new snapshot; blocking computed by a per-profile predicate (`PROFILES`, one entry `spec-panel`: `grade == CRITICAL or rule in {FR-8, FR-9} or (grade == MAJOR and wrong_outcome non-empty)`, `review_ledger.py:41-59`); unknown input keys refused (:809-817); no length limits; missing or ambiguous anchors refuse the whole input (`E-ANCHOR`, `E-ANCHOR-AMBIGUOUS`, :851-881); cap by refusal (`E-CAP`, :1300-1311); body-sha tamper check; one sweep after close; exit codes 0/10/11/12; no multi-reviewer clustering (one input per find) | R02 §6 [CODE-VERIFIED by range reads]; R01 §10.2 |
| stoprule (blind grader) | `~/.claude/commands/sc/spec-panel-stoprule.md` (481); `~/.claude/skills/sc-spec-panel-stoprule-protocol/` (`SKILL.md` 65, `scripts/stoprule.py` 2050, `refs/rubric.md` 15); `~/.claude/agents/finding-grader.md` (35) | sealed claim ledger inside the report; deterministic grade batches with one blocking and one minor canary; the grader sees quote, span, outcome and evidence only, never the reviewer's label or the spec, and decides blocking under rubric B1-B3 (agreement is never a reason); `compute_verdict` is pure over the ledger and "silence never passes" (`stoprule.py:1185-1189`); cap by refusal; no multi-reviewer clustering | R02 §7 [CODE-VERIFIED by range reads] |
| diffgate | `~/.claude/commands/sc/spec-panel-diffgate.md` (481); `~/.claude/skills/sc-diffgate/` (`SKILL.md` 59, `scripts/diffgate.py`) | computes the re-review surface, checks the findings block and fix map, keeps a loop ledger; bodies not read, description only | S05 §1A [UNVERIFIED beyond the description] |

In the variant commands "panel" means the spec-panel expert personas inside one session, not multiple models (R02 §6.1).

**Experiment outcomes and the caveat.** `SNAPSHOT-STATE.txt` says the bundle is "a preservation bundle in progress, not a final success report" and "No valid-success verdict is implied"; diffgate and ponytail repeats are paused for missing owner authorization. `FINAL-REPORT.md:42` says convergence is not proven and `:75` that none of the completed measured loops reached a clean PASS. Per variant: the ledger variant ran one loop with new CRITICAL+MAJOR labels 13, 9 and 3, document growth 22.16% and outcome "ESCALATE; sweep FAIL"; stoprule completed 0 loops (review 1 only, "6 machine-confirmed blockers from 8 sealed claims", provenance check invalid, stopped). The report's own arm table (one scenario, 57,763-byte start spec, 2026-11-08/09; n=2 per PR 427 arm, n=1 per variant) shows every completed loop ending FAIL or ESCALATE; the two pre-427 controls grew the document 57.72% and 69.34%, the exact-427 arms 23.11% and 36.27%, and the variants 10.31% (diffgate), 22.03% (ponytail) and 22.16% (ledger). The only robust observation is therefore smaller document growth under PR 427 and the variants (10 to 36%) than under the pre-427 controls (58 to 69%), not fewer defects. The stoprule loop was invalid because its transcript-integrity verifier failed on asynchronous grader replies; the ponytail final reviewer was requested as `claude-opus-5-5` and recorded as `gpt-6.1-sol` (the same served-model drift seen in E1 and E2); the minfix build halted at task 3. One final review showed six MAJOR labels but four blocking grades, which is direct evidence that label and blocking decision diverge (R02 §8; R11 §11). The variants are therefore candidate designs with partial runs: their code properties are verified by reading, their effect on loop outcomes is not established, and no effort has evidence for rounds 2 and 3 under a multi-reviewer ledger (R02 gap 10, GQ G-22).

**Constraints on plugging in.** The spec-panel Review Loop section is frozen at seven bullets and may not mention a script or parser (`test_review_loop_extension.py:120-127`, `test_section_adds_no_script_or_parser_requirement`); whether that is a deliberate rule is an owner question (R12 summary and gaps). Two blocking rules coexist on master: the prose consequence rule (MAJOR blocks only with a concrete wrong outcome or a security, data-loss or safety risk, `spec-panel.md:259`, prompts `:31`) and the parser rule of findings-v2 (with `reflect_category` set, MAJOR and CRITICAL must be blocking, `findings_v2.py:161-162`) (S05 §2; R05 §10). No spec-review step exists in `sc:brainstorm` or `sc:design` (R09 §6).

### 2.4 The shared review CLI package: two stacks in one package

**Shape.** `src/superclaude/cli/review/` is one click group (`superclaude review`, registered at `cli/main.py:568-570`) that holds two parallel stacks. The #346 v1 stack [E3] (`findings` to `ledger` to `merge_cmd` and `ledger_cmd`, plus `telemetry`; 131 tests) produces verdicts. The reflect v2 stack [E1] (`findings_v2` to `card_convert` and `cluster` to `cluster_cmd` and `verify_cmd`, plus `manifest`; 520 tests) is telemetry and flagging only. `panel.py` is shared by both. The package on this branch equals `origin/master` (d2d8a2d16): `git log d2d8a2d16..HEAD -- src/superclaude/cli/review tests/review` is empty (S02 header). There are seven real subcommands (`panel resolve|validate`, `merge`, `ledger revise|defer|verdict|capture`, `telemetry taskvars|append|load`, `cluster`, `verify-citations`, `manifest init|advance|validate`) plus two ghost loader names, `lint_cmd` and `estimate_cmd`, which belong to unmerged experiment branches PN2 and PN3; the loader swallows the missing module silently; each of the seven real subcommands has its own help-presence test (`test_review_cli.py:44-49` for `panel`, `merge`, `ledger`, `telemetry`; `test_review_cluster_cmd.py:260`; `test_review_verify_citations.py:194`; `test_review_manifest.py:434-439`), but no test pins the exact registered set or the absence of the ghost names (R09 §1 [CODE-VERIFIED]; help tests re-read at HEAD 792cf8c52; D13).

| Module (lines) | Stack | Origin | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `findings.py` (457), `ledger.py` (494), `merge_cmd.py` (118), `ledger_cmd.py` (137) | v1 [E3] | #346 | parse findings-v1, cluster, ledger rows, verdict |
| `telemetry.py` (447), `telemetry_cmd.py` (98) | v1 [E3] | #346 | review-telemetry/1; no caller in `src` |
| `findings_v2.py` (304), `card_convert.py` (517), `cluster.py` (487), `cluster_cmd.py` (197), `verify_cmd.py` (184) | v2 [E1] | reflect (#519) | v2 contract, legacy card conversion, citation clustering, citation pre-check |
| `manifest.py` (534), `manifest_cmd.py` (240) | v2 [E1] | reflect (#519) | staged run manifest |
| `panel.py` (707), `panel_cmd.py` (129), 8 `data/review-panel.*.json`, `review-tiers.default.json` | shared | #346 plus reflect additions | template and tier resolution |

(S02 §1 [CODE-VERIFIED].) The v2 stack imports private v1 names (`_check_flat`, `_ID`, `_blocks_after`, `_HEAD_FINDINGS`) and the public `refs_norm` and `flat` from `findings.py`, so a change to the v1 limits or fence rules changes v2 too; the numbers 12, 200, 300 and 8 are repeated as literals in nine places with no shared constant (R01 §14.1). There is no v2 ledger, v2 verdict or v2 merged report (S02 §1 observations).

**Today's data flow, stack A: findings-v1 to verdict [E3] (also the stack E2 drove unchanged).**

```
 reviewer report (fresh context, same brief)  ->  "## Findings block" with ```findings-v1 JSON lines
        |
        v
 findings.parse_block      10 ordered rules per line (findings.py:90-121)
        |   bad line -> skipped, first error kept, block_ok=false; the other lines are KEPT
        v
 findings.annotate         anchor located by flattened exact match in ONE candidate document
        |   missing anchor -> kept, span None, section "none"                       (D5)
        v
 findings.cluster          union-find, transitive: same fp (section+refs) OR refs intersect
        |                  and spans within 3 lines; no chain detection              (D6)
        v
 ledger.merge_round        row.blocking = any(member.blocking)                       (D4)
        |   clearing loop: resolved_check rows nobody re-reported -> resolved,
        |   block_ok never read                                                      (D2)
        |   raises only if NO reviewer block is valid                                (D3)
        v
 verdict  = FAIL iff any open|regressed blocking row          (ledger.py:273-274)
 decision = PASS | REVISE (n < cap) | ESCALATE                (label only; round 4 merges)
        |
        v
 merged report + reviser brief -> reviser -> fixmap-v1 -> `review ledger revise` -> next round
```
(R01 §1; R02 §1.2; R03 §1-3; S02 §3 [CODE-VERIFIED]. Not drawn: the installed experiment ledger and stoprule, which are variants of this loop, section 2.3.)

**Today's data flow, stack B: findings-v2 to telemetry, beside the authoritative legacy verdict [E1].**

```
 reviewer card (reflect-reviewer, persona) = legacy card + "## Findings block" (findings-v2)
        |                                    + calibration.per_finding (blind calibrator line)
        |
        +--> findings_v2.parse_block     23 ordered rules per line (findings_v2.py:84-187)
        |        ANY bad line -> block state "invalid"
        |        -> cluster_v2 skips EVERY finding of a non-complete block (cluster.py:221, :256-257)
        |    cluster_v2          citation-based union-find; `chained` flag; calibrated `support`;
        |                        `disputed`; cluster_agreement; anchor-only findings stay singletons
        |    verify-citations    flags citations to re-read, drops nothing
        |        ==> panel/clusters.json + telemetry: block   TELEMETRY ONLY, never routes or drops
        |
        +--> legacy path (authoritative; protocol steps executed by the orchestrator)
                 sc-adversarial Mode A over the card files -> adversarial/merged-verdict.yaml
                 -> evidence-validator -> return-contract.yaml (1.8.0, orchestrator-written)
                 -> contract.derive_verdict: HALTED on regression or drift count > 0,
                    DEGRADED on convergence < 0.80 or null, else PASS
```
(R01 §2; R03 §2; R05 §1, §7, §9; R07 §1; S02 §3 [CODE-VERIFIED for the CLI and wrapper steps; the debate, evidence-validator and contract writing are protocol-executed and checked on disk by `panel_lint` EV-1, R07 §2.3, rather than by a Python orchestrator].)

**Key divergences between the two stacks (all [CODE-VERIFIED]).**

**The third merge path: the code-driven Tier 2 engine behind the blocking post gate [E1-adjacent: master baseline].** `superclaude reflect run` accepts only `--depth standard|deep` (`commands.py:255`), and `runner.py:538-545` always calls `run_tier2_ensemble` for those depths and then sets `rc = 0` unconditionally, so the `/sc:reflect` skill, its 1.8.0 contract, `panel_lint` and the shadow kernel are never involved in the gate (R13 §2.1, §2.4 [CODE-VERIFIED]). Provenance contradiction: the task scheme tags `cli/reflect/` code [E1], but `git diff --stat origin/master` over `ensemble.py`, `runner.py`, `contract.py`, `commands.py`, `config.py` is empty and `git log` shows PRs #213, #214, #220 and #329, so the engine predates the E1 shadow work and is master baseline; the stronger evidence is the diff, so this file calls it E1-adjacent (R13 §1.7).

| Verdict | deviation fields default clean (:103-113, :442-471), so no production contract can HALT on a found deviation; the gate is a reviewer-agreement and diversity check, not a deviation audit | R13 §10 D1 (graded Critical) |

Two reflect contract schemas therefore share one file name and one reader (`contract.py`): the skill's 1.8.0 contract written by the orchestrator and this engine's code-written "1.0" (R13 gap 15, R08 §12).

**Reading the matrix.** The efforts overlap most (same purpose) on the finding contract, severity scale, limits, clustering, merge, verdict, panel templates, tier configuration, identity, dispatch, brief, telemetry and evaluation. They agree on data contract only for the severity tuple and the panel template schema, and on code only for `panel.py`, the v1 primitives that v2 imports, and the tests directory. No component is implemented identically by two efforts, and four components have only one owner: the shadow harness (E1), the blind-judge benchmark (E2), the ledger verify-only and blind-grader mechanisms (E3 experiments) and the run manifest (E1). None of the three ledgers combines multi-reviewer clustering with an independent blocking decision (R02 §7.3 [CODE-VERIFIED]).

Only [CODE-VERIFIED] statements are presented as current. |

- **Desired behavior:** One central Review Panel made of a shared core plus thin per-use-case modules. The shared core is the `src/superclaude/cli/review/` package (E3 v1 stack plus the E1 v2 stack) extended with: one finding contract with pluggable lens namespaces, one clusterer, one merge and verdict stage that separates "candidate" from "blocking", one run record, one code-rendered brief template, and a resolver that declares distinctness and records observed identity. Each thin module owns only what differs per consumer: lens name, severity scale and category map, primary location kind, id grammar, blocking predicate, brief slot values, and the advisory-or-blocking policy. The core serves five consumers (below). This is a target derived from the research design inputs (`research/02` section 9, `03` Q9, `04` section 10, `06` section 6, `08` section 11.3, `09` section 8, `10` section 5, `01` section 18); no research file shows it implemented.

### 3.1 External context used by Section 3 (web research, not codebase fact)

| Topic | Finding | Source URL | Reliability noted by the research |
|---|---|---|---|
| Union vs weighted voting | Any-reviewer ("union") voting: 82.7% recall, 85.0% false-positive rate vs weighted voting 37.7% recall, 35.3% FPR (vulnerability detection). | https://arxiv.org/html/2602.17875v1 | preprint, Feb 2026 [external context, `web-01`] |
| LLM validators | Validators confirm but rarely reject (TPR above 96%, TNR below 25%); a calibrated minority veto beat majority vote. | https://arxiv.org/html/2510.11822v2 | preprint, Oct 2025 [external context, `web-01`] |
| Panels vs single judge | Heterogeneous panels beat one large judge on average (PoLL), but judge errors are correlated (9 judges gave about 2 effective votes). | https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.18796 ; https://arxiv.org/html/2605.29800v1 | [external context, `web-01`, `web-03`] |
| Debate vs meta-judge | Debate amplifies judge bias after round one; meta-judge aggregation is more resistant (accuracy not measured). | https://arxiv.org/html/2505.19477v3 | EMNLP 2025 Findings [external context, `web-01`] |
| Production review systems | Reviewers propose; a coordinator or verifier deduplicates, verifies against source and applies a severity rubric before anything blocks; singletons are verified, not discarded. | https://blog.cloudflare.com/ai-code-review ; https://www.linkedin.com/blog/engineering/ai/high-signal-ai-code-review-that-adapts-to-your-codebase-at-scale ; https://cursor.com/blog/building-bugbot | vendor first-party, no error rates [external context, `web-01`] |
| Severity interchange | SARIF `level` has three buckets (error, warning, note) and `rank` 0-100 is the lossless order; every 3-to-5 or 5-to-3 mapping loses a tier at the extremes; the middle tier is kept distinct everywhere except our `card_convert` (`medium` to MINOR). | https://docs.oasis-open.org/sarif/sarif/v2.1.0/sarif-v2.1.0.html ; https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/reference/code-scanning/sarif-files/sarif-support | official standard and vendor docs [external context, `web-02`] |
| Finding identity across commits | GitHub code scanning matches alerts only via `partialFingerprints.primaryLocationLineHash` plus rule id and path; an empty hash degrades to order-based matching. Transitive closure has high recall and poor precision ("black hole" clusters); complete-link or size caps are the documented remedies. | https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/reference/code-scanning/sarif-files/sarif-support ; https://github.com/github/codeql-action/blob/main/src/fingerprints.ts | official docs and source [external context, `web-04`] |
| Judge calibration | Self-preference and same-family bias are real but partly an artefact; verbalized numeric confidence is weakly discriminative; no controlled study of heterogeneous panels for defect-finding or spec review was found, so the project's own labelled packages are the validation set. | https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22548 ; https://arxiv.org/html/2611.01829v1 | preprints [external context, `web-03`] |

## 4. Gap Analysis

**Rule applied to this table (verbatim):** 'Docs may not close a defect (C8, behavioral-reachability control). A gap that is an UNWIRED IN-SCOPE capability — one the driving spec/TDD names as shipped or enabled-by-config but that is NOT actually wired at its runtime entrypoint (no production caller, its result discarded/dead-guarded, or its callee a not-implemented sentinel) — is a DEFECT, not merely future-phase work. It MUST be recorded with Severity Critical/High, MUST carry (or link) an MDTM remediation task under .dev/tasks/to-do/, and MUST NOT be silently downgraded to future phase / later release / Open Question without an on-record, cited scope decision.'

**How the rule is applied in this run.** The run is report-only (owner scope change 2026-11-13). Every row that is an unwired in-scope capability is recorded as Severity Critical, is tagged with the migration track (M1-M4) whose Section 8 steps will wire it (Section 8 is written later by synth-06, which must cover every Critical or Important row of this table), and carries the note `remediation task to be created after the merge of the two reports; none created in this run (owner scope: report only)`. Rows carrying the C8 note: D14, MS-11, MS-14, ENS-1, ENS-3, ENS-4, ENS-5 (restated as doc contradictions DOC-20, DOC-63, DOC-64 and DOC-65 in group (v)). For each, the row cites the document that names the capability as live and the code that shows it unwired; where the research did not establish the "driving spec names it as shipped" premise, the row says so and the point is also carried to Open Questions (Section 9; for D14 this is question Q-58).

**Row groups.** (i) D1-D16, the hand-off defects checked against current code. (ii) BL-nn, blockers for PR code review and for rf-qa / rf-qa-qualitative replacement (each row names the consumers it blocks). (iii) MS-nn, missing shared pieces, consumer hooks and reflect-side gaps. (iv) ENS-nn, the code-driven tasklist post gate (`ensemble.py`). (v) DOC-nn, one row per [CODE-CONTRADICTED] or [STALE DOC] finding (same number as log row `D-nn`). (vi) OPEN-nn, further Important gaps of the log not already carried. The origin tag [E1] [E2] [E3] [cross] follows the Track tag in Notes.

## 5. External Research Findings

This section is supplementary external context gathered from the web; where it differs from the codebase findings in Sections 1-4, the codebase findings take precedence.

### Reading notes (apply to every table in 5.1 to 5.5)

| Item | Meaning |
|---|---|
| EXTERNAL | Every finding in this section comes from the web research files and is external context, not a statement about our code. |
| Source verification tags | `[E]` page extracted (full or excerpt) by the research agent; `[A]` abstract only; `[S]` search snippet only (lower confidence); `[2]` numbers taken from a secondary summary, not the primary paper; `[V]` vendor first-party page; `[U]` unverified claim. |
| Relationship values | `supports`, `extends`, `contradicts`, as the research files assign them. Where a research file says "partly", it is kept in the cell. |
| D-codes (D1, D2/D3, D4, D5, D6, D9) | Defect labels as used inside the cited research files; their definitions and resolution live in the conflict log (synth-04), not here. |
| C-codes (C1 to C5 in web-01; C4 in web-03) | Codebase-context facts that the web research agent copied from research/02, research/05 and research/11; they are not independent evidence. |
| Domain caveat | Almost no external source measured spec or tasklist review with a panel; most measured code, QA, NLI, vulnerability detection or feedback validity. Direction transfers by analogy; magnitudes do not. |

### 5.1 Multi-reviewer panel aggregation

Source file: `research/web-01-panel-aggregation.md` (Tavily; sections 1, 3 and 4 of that file). The jury-versus-single-judge and judge-bias material of web-01 section 2 is reported in 5.3 because it concerns who judges.

#### 5.1.1 Aggregation rules and measured error rates

| Finding | Source | Date | Relevance | Relationship to codebase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Union voting ("any reviewer flags") in a zero-shot multi-agent vulnerability ensemble gave 82.7% recall, 48.8% precision and 85.0% false-positive rate; weighted voting gave 37.7% recall with 35.3% false-positive rate. Authors call 85% FPR the main deployment constraint and unsuitable for CI gating. | https://arxiv.org/html/2602.17875v1 (MultiVer; preprint) `[S]`; exact numbers MEDIUM confidence until extracted | Feb 2026 | HIGH | supports. The ledger rule "row blocking = any member blocking" (C1, research/02) maximises recall at the cost of precision; direction matches the measured 65 versus 38 blocking result (research/05). Domain is vulnerability classification, so direction transfers, magnitude does not. |
| Cross-judge majority voting (self-judge excluded) reduces leniency but treats all judges as equally reliable; calibrated weighted majority voting weights each vote by an online estimate of that judge's error rates from inter-judge agreement and tracked an oracle within 0.5 percentage points in simulation. | https://arxiv.org/html/2609.12002v1 (preprint) `[E]` | Sep 2026 (arXiv id) | HIGH | extends. Our `confidence` field is a count of distinct reviewers that no decision reads (C1; research/02 D4: displayed, not decision-bearing). Evidence for the weighted rule is simulation-only: an option, not a proven rule. |
| Self-aggregation of the same LLM over several runs (Self-Agg, n=10, Gemini-2.5-Flash) raised F1 to 21.91% (+43.67%) and recall to 30.44% (+118.83%); the gain is mostly recall and absolute F1 stays low. A secondary summary says F1 plateaus near 5-10 runs. | https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.01494 (SWR-Bench; preprint) `[S]`; plateau claim https://zylos.ai/research/2026-03-01-multi-model-ai-code-review-convergence `[2]` | Sep 2025; secondary 2026-03-01 | MEDIUM | extends. Aggregation does not evidence that false blockers go away; a blocking gate on raw aggregated findings would over-block. |
| Fourteen LLM validators had true-positive rate above 96% but true-negative rate typically below 25% (they confirm and rarely reject). Majority vote "is not good enough". A minority veto (mark invalid if at least 4 of 14 say so) gave the lowest maximum error: 2.8% after data repair, TPR 95.5%, TNR 30.9%; the n=4 threshold itself needed a human-labelled calibration set. Minority veto was robust to missing votes; a super-majority rule that defaults a missing vote to "invalid" did slightly worse. A regression bias model on a small labelled set reached 1.2% maximum absolute error. | https://arxiv.org/html/2510.11822v2 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11822 (OpenReview https://openreview.net/forum?id=3IsAoRHi9n; preprint) `[E]` | Oct 2025 | HIGH | extends and partly cautions. Reverse polarity of our ledger (there one reviewer can assert blocking, C1). Shows a lenient grader is a weak precision filter, so the blind grader (C5) needs a measured true-negative rate. The "missing vote counted as an answer" shape is D2/D3 (an invalid reviewer counted as no finding, C3). Task is feedback validity, so transfer is by analogy. |
| In requirement-conformance checks LLMs over-reject correct code; asking them to explain and propose a fix raised misjudgment. A reviewer can be right for the wrong reason: GPT-4o symptom-level match 98.2% on HumanEval versus bug-cause match 59.1%. | https://arxiv.org/html/2603.00539v1 `[E]`; journal version https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10515-026-00638-5 | Mar 2026; journal 2026 | HIGH | supports. Direction of the measured wrong-blocker problem (65 versus 38, research/05). Suggests a cause-level evidence check (our citation and anchor checks) is worth more than another reviewer's opinion. Benchmarks are small coding sets, not spec review. |

#### 5.1.2 Multi-agent review systems in production

| Finding | Source | Date | Relevance | Relationship to codebase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cursor Bugbot early pipeline: eight parallel passes with randomised diff order, bucket similar bugs, majority vote to drop bugs seen in one pass, merge buckets, filter categories, validator model for false positives, dedupe against bugs already posted. Largest later gains came from a fully agentic redesign; whether majority voting survived is not stated `[U]`. Resolution rate 52% to 70% is a secondary, self-reported figure and is a resolution-by-merge metric, not a false-positive rate. | https://cursor.com/blog/building-bugbot `[V][E]`; secondary https://victorinollc.com/thinking/ai-code-review-bugbot, https://www.spotdev.co.uk/blog/cursor-bugbot-ai-code-review `[2]` | Date not shown (refs "this fall"); secondary 2026 | HIGH | extends. Dedupe against earlier runs is the same job as our cross-round row matching (research/02, ledger.py:166-171). Bugbot passes are one model with shuffled input, so a singleton there is more likely noise than in a heterogeneous panel (web-01 inference, see 5.1.4). |
| Cloudflare: up to seven specialised reviewers in parallel; a coordinator deduplicates, re-categorises and applies a reasonableness filter (reads source when unsure). Approval is a fixed rubric: any critical item or production safety risk gives "significant concerns" and blocks; several warnings revoke approval; one warning in a clean change still gets "approved with comments". Bias toward approval is stated explicitly. | https://blog.cloudflare.com/ai-code-review `[V][E]` | Date not shown | HIGH | supports. A single adjudicator, not the reviewers, decides blocking from a severity rubric after a verification filter; reflect's blocking classes Drift and Regression (C4, research/05) are the same pattern. Differs: a single warning never blocks there. Our ledger states no verdict bias. |
| LinkedIn: each subagent (a distinct model-and-harness pairing) reviews the full diff blind to the others; a finding raised by two or more is elevated as high-confidence; a one-model finding is not discarded but sent for verification and rated separately. | https://www.linkedin.com/blog/engineering/ai/high-signal-ai-code-review-that-adapts-to-your-codebase-at-scale `[V][E]` | Date not shown | HIGH | supports using overlap (our `confidence` overlap versus single, display-only per C1) as a routing input to verification, not a drop rule and not ignored. contradicts the Bugbot-style drop-singletons rule for heterogeneous panels. |
| 294 human-confirmed defects over 33 artifacts, fifteen model versions from eight providers: no large-sample model exceeded about 61% code recall; 56.8% (167 of 294) of confirmed defects were found by exactly one model; median pairwise cross-family Jaccard about 0.29; coverage rose from about 47% (one reviewer) to about 72% (two), with diminishing returns after. Authors recommend two or three independent reviewers plus a human verifying against source. | https://zenodo.org/records/21328807 (self-published, single team corpus) `[A]` | Reviews dated Apr-Jul 2026 | HIGH (reliability LOW to MEDIUM) | supports keeping a union-of-reviewers candidate set (C1 recall) and contradicts a hard quorum as the only blocking gate: requiring agreement would have dropped more than half the confirmed defects in this corpus. Also supports reflect degrading a single-reviewer merge (C4, contract.py:295-296), since the second reviewer adds the most. |
| Ensembles are mostly run for recall and false positives stack with each reviewer; the cost of a false positive depends on whether a human or an agent reads it next. A figure of 93.4% unique issues with no same-line overlap across four parallel reviewers is second-hand and unverified. | https://dev.to/pyor/multiple-ai-code-reviewers-do-parallel-bots-help-57ag `[2][U]`; https://www.augmentcode.com/guides/deep-code-review-recall-vs-precision `[V]` | Aug (year not shown); guide updated Aug 2026 | MEDIUM (reliability LOW) | extends. Supports a two-stage design (wide candidate set, then verification) over a stronger vote at the first stage. |
| Mozilla.ai Star Chamber: several providers with no cross-visibility; issues classed consensus (all), majority (two or more) or individual (one provider, "may be a specialised insight, or may be noise"); JSON output with typed severity, file:line and category so grouping uses location and category, not fuzzy text. Ellipsis (via ZenML summary): parallel generators then dedup, confidence threshold, a hallucination filter that checks each comment against its evidence, and editing. | https://blog.mozilla.ai/the-star-chamber-multi-llm-consensus-for-code-quality; https://www.zenml.io/llmops-database/building-and-deploying-production-llm-code-review-agents-architecture-and-best-practices `[V]` | Date not shown; Ellipsis 2024 | MEDIUM | supports our typed finding contract and anchor and citation checks as the enabling condition for reliable clustering (research/02 section 1). The Ellipsis evidence filter is the opposite of our rule that a finding whose anchor is absent from the document still becomes an open blocking row (test at tests/review/test_review_ledger.py:408-417, D5). |

#### 5.1.3 Deduplicating findings across reviewers

| Finding | Source | Date | Relevance | Relationship to codebase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shared production sequence: cluster findings describing the same problem; keep the merged item once where it fits best; keep every contributing finder id and dimension on the merged record; let a verifier's severity override the finder's self-assessment; drop refuted items and carry "uncertain" with a reason; dedupe again against earlier runs; group on typed location and category. | Cursor, Cloudflare, LinkedIn, Mozilla.ai (above) plus https://forum.level1techs.com/t/how-i-do-llm-assisted-code-reviews/250113 (forum, LOW) | Dates not shown | HIGH (vendor blogs MEDIUM, forum LOW) | supports our member tracking, previous-ledger row matching (ledger.py:166-171) and the same-defect fingerprint. extends: "verifier severity overrides reviewer severity" is not in the ledger (blocking is any member's flag, C1) and is a ready-made alternative to the any-member rule. |
| Generic embedding-based semantic dedup: embed, k-means cluster, pairwise cosine inside clusters, threshold, keep one representative. | https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/curator/curate-text/process-data/deduplication/semdedup (NeMo Curator docs) `[V]` | Date not shown | LOW | extends only as a fallback to anchor-and-fingerprint matching; documented for dataset curation, no over-merge risk analysis for distinct defects. |

#### 5.1.4 Within-5.1 conflicts and evidence gaps

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Singleton handling splits the field | Cursor drops findings seen in one pass; LinkedIn verifies them; the Zenodo corpus says most true defects are singletons across families. Web-01 reconciles them by an inference of its own, stated by none of the sources: with homogeneous passes a singleton is likelier noise, with heterogeneous reviewers likelier a real catch. Treat the reconciliation as an unverified hypothesis. Stronger evidence: the Zenodo corpus (measured, but LOW to MEDIUM reliability); Cursor and LinkedIn are first-party design descriptions without error rates. |
| Codebase-side inconsistency noted by web-01 | Reflect degrades a single-reviewer merge (contract.py:295-296) while the ledger passes a round on one valid reviewer (ledger.py:150-157, pinned at tests/review/test_review_ledger.py:385), as recorded in research/02 and research/05. External evidence (Zenodo coverage step, Nine Judges in 5.3) supports treating one reviewer as insufficient for a PASS. Resolution belongs to synth-04. |
| Wording discrepancy | The note that `confidence` is "computed but unused" is only partly true (research/02 D4: displayed, not decision-bearing). External sources treat overlap count as a decision or routing input, so this is a design choice, not a code error. |
| Gap: no measured clustering error | No peer-reviewed measurement of over-merge or under-merge rates when clustering findings from several LLM reviewers, nor of how clustering errors change a blocking verdict. Dedup evidence is practitioner description. |
| Gap: no spec or tasklist panel study | No source evaluated blocking decisions on non-code documents with a panel. |

#### 5.1.5 External-research options for the merge and blocking rule (from web-01; options, not decisions)

| # | Option | Basis in 5.1 |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Split "candidate" from "blocking": keep a wide any-reviewer candidate set, make a finding blocking only after verification against source (anchor and citation checks first, then an independent adjudicator). This would replace the any-member rule as the decider while keeping it as the candidate filter. | Cloudflare, LinkedIn, Cursor validator, over-rejection study, Zenodo |
| 2 | No hard N-of-M quorum as the only gate; use reviewer overlap to route and prioritise (verify singletons, rank overlaps first); wire the existing display-only `confidence` field into that routing. | Zenodo 56.8% singletons; Nine Judges (5.3) |
| 3 | Treat an invalid or truncated reviewer block as an abstention that counts against the quorum of valid reviewers, not "no findings"; a PASS needs at least two valid reviewers, a FAIL needs one verified blocking finding. Web-01 marks this as its own inference; it would change the assertion at tests/review/test_review_ledger.py:385 on purpose. | Agreeableness study (missing-vote handling), Zenodo second-reviewer step |
| 4 | Tune any vote threshold (for example promoting a verified singleton) on human labels; consider per-reviewer reliability weights only after a calibration set exists (simulation-only evidence). | Agreeableness study; weighted-vote preprint |
| 5 | Dedup on typed fields (location, category, anchor), keep every contributing reviewer id, let the verifier's severity override a reviewer's self-assigned severity, dedupe across rounds; embedding similarity fallback only. | Section 5.1.3 |
| 6 | State the verdict bias explicitly and record per round how many blockers were dropped at verification. | Cloudflare |
| 7 | Measure outcome (share of blocking findings fixed or upheld), not volume; caveat: Cursor's metric is self-reported and is not a false-positive rate. | Cursor |
| 8 | Panel size: three heterogeneous reviewers plus one adjudicator is the evidence-supported size; more needs measured error independence. | Zenodo diminishing returns; Nine Judges |

### 5.2 Severity taxonomies and harmonization

Source file: `research/web-02-severity-harmonization.md` (Tavily). Codebase facts that file marks CODE-VERIFIED (from research/01 and research/10): findings-v1/v2 use three severities (CRITICAL, MAJOR, MINOR) and MINOR can never be blocking, with `blocking` a reviewer-written bool; reflect legacy cards use HIGH/MEDIUM/LOW and card_convert maps `high` to MAJOR plus blocking, and `medium`, `low` and `important` to MINOR non-blocking; rf-qa uses CRITICAL/IMPORTANT/MINOR and blocks "by definition, not by the label"; Auggie and PR review use Critical/High/Medium/Low/Nit with blocking derived from the remapped level; the review-loop prose has a fourth grade "Medium" meaning "any label with blocking false".

| Finding | Source | Date | Relevance | Relationship to codebase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SARIF `level` has four values: `error` (serious problem), `warning` (problem found), `note` (minor problem or improvement opportunity) and `none` (severity does not apply because `kind` is not `fail`). `kind` values: fail (default), pass, open, informational, notApplicable. | https://docs.oasis-open.org/sarif/sarif/v2.1.0/sarif-v2.1.0.html (OASIS SARIF 2.1.0 Errata 01, sections 3.27.9-3.27.10) `[E]`, official standard | Date not shown | HIGH | supports keeping severity and result kind as two orthogonal fields; `none` plus `kind` is the standard's way to carry non-defects, which fits the findings-v2 channel split (defect, grounding-gap, advisory). `note` covers MINOR and PR Low and Nit together. |
| SARIF `rank` is a 0.0-100.0 priority, meaningful only when `kind` is fail, derived from `level` when absent; the spec gives no bucket boundaries. | Same spec, sections 3.27.25 and 3.50.4 `[E]` | Date not shown | HIGH | extends. Standard lossless slot for finer order inside a 3-bucket `level`. Our findings have no numeric priority field (CODE-VERIFIED absent in v1/v2); our core would own the cut-point table. |

#### 5.2.3 Cross-tool equivalence and lossless-mapping strategies

Cross-tool equivalence (web-02 section 6.5; documented vendor values, row alignment is the research agent's judgment where no vendor mapping exists):

| Rank | SARIF level | GitHub | Semgrep | SonarQube (legacy / MQR) | CodeRabbit | OWASP | GitLab |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | error (rank high) | critical (over 9.0) | CRITICAL | Blocker | Critical | Critical | Critical (rank 90-100) |
| 2 | error | high (7.0-8.9) | HIGH (= legacy ERROR) | Critical / High | Major | High | High |
| 3 | warning | medium (4.0-6.9) | MEDIUM (= WARNING) | Major / Medium | Minor | Medium | Medium |
| 4 | note | low (0.1-3.9) | LOW (= INFO) | Minor / Low | Trivial | Low | Low |
| 5 | note (rank low) / none | none | none | Info | Info | Note | Info |

Strategies observed (web-02 section 7.2) and what each keeps or risks:

| # | Strategy | Used by | Keeps | Loses or risks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | Coarse ordinal plus finer numeric field | SARIF rank, GitLab | Order inside a bucket; a fifth tier above `error` | `rank` has no standard cut points |
| S2 | Severity from impact and likelihood, confidence separate | Semgrep, OWASP, GitHub precision | Why the severity is what it is | Needs two reviewer inputs; none carried today |
| S3 | Obligation separate from severity | Conventional Comments, GitHub gate, Google | Policy changes without re-grading | Free-form obligation can contradict severity (needs a validation rule such as "MINOR cannot block") |
| S4 | Legacy alias table with versioning | Semgrep, SonarQube 10.2 | Old reports keep working | Aliases land mid-scale; Sonar's extreme collapse later called "not ideal" |
| S5 | Native value preserved in a named property | SARIF converter guidance | Exact round trip | Not comparable across tools without a core value |
| S6 | Category-kind-specific scale with a bridge | CodeQL, SonarQube MQR | Each family keeps its natural scale | Two scales to explain; the bridge must carry category |
| S7 | Visibility policy on top of severity | CodeRabbit, GitHub gate | Nothing dropped from storage | Policy lives outside the finding, so exports lose it unless recorded |

Collapse analysis: a 5-to-3 collapse (Critical and High to error, Medium to warning, Low and Nit to note) is not invertible (`error` could be Critical or High; `note` could be Low or Nit); 3-to-5-to-3 is lossless only if the five-level value or `rank` is kept, 5-to-3-to-5 never is. Our PR router has three routes (Critical/High deep fix, Medium fix, Low/Nit report-only; severity_router.py:203-223, research/10), which line up with error/warning/note, so `level` suffices for routing but not for the PR rubric's own Critical versus High distinction (severity-rubric.md:11-61, per web-02).

Where our five vocabularies lose information when mapped to a candidate core (web-02 section 8; the mapping is the research agent's proposal, not stated by any source; full 19-row table in that file):

| Where | Loss | External-research handling |
|---|---|---|
| Review-loop "Medium" (MAJOR label with blocking false) and reflect `MEDIUM` | The medium tier exists only as prose, a card_convert collapse to MINOR, and a PR tier; whether a medium reflect drift blocks is UNDECIDED (an owner decision, not settled by external sources) | Keep `medium` as its own tier; store the native label |
| Reflect deviation classes Authorized expansion and Necessary deviation | Non-defects; forcing a severity inflates counts | Keep as class field with non-defect kind (SARIF `kind` precedent) |
| rf-qa `IMPORTANT` | rf-qa blocks by definition, not label; collides with card_convert `important` to MINOR non-blocking (card_convert.py:82) | Carry `blocking` separately |
| v1 CRITICAL with blocking false | v1 bars only MINOR from blocking (findings.py:100-101) | Keep both fields and flag the contradictory pair |
| Low versus Nit; Critical versus High at `level` layer | Not distinguishable in SARIF `level` | Keep core ordinal or `rank` |
| Codex P0-P3 | Priority, not severity; definitions unverified | Keep as native hint with its own table |

### 5.3 LLM-as-judge and calibration

Source files: `research/web-03-judge-calibration.md` (all sections) and `research/web-01-panel-aggregation.md` section 2 (juries versus single judges). Codebase context recorded in web-03 from research/05 and research/11: reflect requires the calibrator from a different model class than the reviewer; the calibrator agent is written for a 6-dimension troubleshoot rubric while reflect uses 5 dimensions; legacy recorded cards held 0 numeric per-finding calibrations of 689 findings, while shadow runs hold 142 of 142 (research/05 section 5; web-03 line 11 states the shadow figure as 0 of 689, a slip not carried here); the other session scored panels with a blind Opus judge over anonymised merged reports; the E2 judge was blind to reviewer ids but NOT to panel name (research/11 section 2: the judge-one.sh schema contains the combo name, which encodes model names); an experiment grader is blind with a frozen rubric (blocking yes or no); reflect degrades single-reviewer merges and convergence below 0.80 (contract.py).

#### 5.3.1 Panels versus single judges (who judges)

| Finding | Source | Date | Relevance | Relationship to codebase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A panel of three smaller judges from disjoint model families (Command R, GPT-3.5, Haiku) beat a single large judge (GPT-4) on agreement with humans across three judge settings and six datasets, showed less intra-model bias and cost over seven times less. Kappa on KILT-NQ 0.763 versus 0.627 `[2]`; GPT-4 kappa moved 0.518 to 0.725 with prompt wording `[2]`; panel selection left as future work; QA-style correctness only, not code review. | https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.18796 (PoLL, Verga et al.) `[A]`; numbers via https://liner.com/review/replacing-judges-with-juries-evaluating-llm-generations-with-panel-diverse, https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2404.18796 `[2]` | 29 Apr 2024 | HIGH in web-03, MEDIUM in web-01 (task mismatch) | supports a heterogeneous panel with cheap members and the class-disjoint rule (t2_model_class_diversity == full, contract.py:282-284, research/05). contradicts, per web-03, the single blind Opus judge as the one decider (the configuration PoLL argues against), though that judge scores panels offline and does not decide verdicts. extends: reviewer agreement can play the calibrator's role. |
| Nine frontier LLMs from seven families on three NLI datasets gave about 2 effective independent votes (Kish effective sample size 2.0-2.5); panel accuracy fell 8-22 points below independent voting; the best single judge matched or beat the full panel in every condition; extra judges or smarter aggregation closed at most 11% of the gap. Same-family error correlation (phi 0.437, 0.435) barely exceeded cross-family (0.389); the three most correlated pairs were cross-family (Claude x Gemini 0.603). The authors note PoLL compares with the average judge, not the best. | https://arxiv.org/html/2605.29800v1 and https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/correlated-llm-evaluation-panels `[E]` preprint | May 2026 | HIGH | contradicts a naive reading of heterogeneity as a guarantee. Our diversity gate counts classes and vendors (contract.py:282-288, research/05), which measures label diversity, not error independence. A 2-of-3 quorum may behave like about 2 votes; compare the panel with its best single reviewer in telemetry. Tasks are NLI and preference, not code review. |
| Apollo Research: judges differ systematically in severity (some score high, Claude models more conservative); Anthropic models' judgments are very similar, so correlated models add little; ensembles with monitors from different providers calibrate better; no single model matched the reference; synthetic injected failures, reference labels from a multi-model pipeline. | https://www.apolloresearch.ai/monitoring/evaluating-llm-calibration-for-coding-agent-monitoring `[E][V]` | Date not shown (post-2025) `[U]` | HIGH | supports vendor-level, not only class-level, diversity for the calibrator: Opus and Sonnet judging each other are one correlated family. Sharpens "different model class than the reviewer"; the contract already tracks `t2_vendor_diversity` (research/05 section 1.3). Mixed panels need per-model severity anchoring or a rank-based merge rather than raw severity averaging. |

#### 5.3.4 Calibration methods and practice

| Finding | Source | Date | Relevance | Relationship to codebase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Platt scaling suits monotone miscalibration; isotonic regression is non-parametric but overfits small sets (blogs cite roughly 1000+ examples; one study fitted on 60); fit on a calibration split, refit when model, prompt or distribution changes; a blog claim that Platt on 200+ examples cuts ECE 30-60% is marketing-style and excluded. Isotonic reward calibration for judge scores uses a small labelled slice with a fallback for response-length bias. | https://www.kdnuggets.com/a-deep-dive-into-calibration-of-language-models-platt-scaling-isotonic-regression-temperature-scaling; https://futureagi.com/blog/evaluating-llm-confidence-uncertainty-2026 (blogs, LOW); https://arxiv.org/html/2512.11150v1 `[S]` | Dec 2025 (arXiv); blogs 2026 | MEDIUM | extends. Against the real data a fit is not currently possible: the 689 legacy findings carry no numbers and no ground truth, the 142 shadow numbers carry no ground truth, and the E2 labelled packages carry no calibrator numbers (research/05 section 5); a fit needs numbers and labels on the same findings, so it waits for a run that produces both. Even then it holds only for a fixed model-prompt pair; because panel models change (fallback ladders, combo experiments), a fitted mapping goes stale, which argues against a numeric calibrator in the shared core until composition stabilises. |
| Practice descriptions: a confidence filter between review engine and comment publisher with category-specific thresholds; deterministic-rule findings pass unconditionally; suppressed findings logged to tune thresholds; adversarial review (proposer, challenger on a different vendor, arbiter) for false positives; a verification stack's false-negative rate is invisible unless a random sample of passing output is audited; thresholds drift permissive under one-sided pressure of visible false positives. | https://dev.to/dextralabs/how-to-build-a-custom-ai-code-review-agent-for-proprietary-codebases-329c; https://heym.run/blog/ai-code-review; https://sourcegraph.com/blog/automated-code-review-tools; https://hidekazu-konishi.com/entry/llm_output_verification_patterns.html `[S]` | 2026 | LOW to MEDIUM | supports calibration as a pluggable filter whose suppressed items are logged (the telemetry role); extends: a standing audit sample of passed or suppressed items. Practice description, not independent evidence. |
| Evidence gap: no controlled study of heterogeneous reviewer panels merged by a fuser for code or spec defect-finding; the closest are PoLL (correctness), the fuser paper (pairwise judging) and the code-evaluation bias paper. | web-03 section 6.5 | 2026-11-14 | HIGH (limits confidence) | extends: the panel's merge-and-grade design is an extrapolation; the project's own labelled packages are the real validation set. |

#### 5.3.5 Within-5.3 conflicts and gaps

| Conflict | Detail and which side is stronger |
|---|---|
| Panel versus best single judge | PoLL (2024, abstract primary, numbers secondary, correctness scoring, weaker judges) says a diverse panel beats one large judge. Nine Judges (May 2026, extracted, frontier models) says nine judges gave about 2 effective votes and the best single judge matched or beat the panel, noting PoLL compares with the average judge. Nine Judges is more recent and uses current-class models; PoLL is the better-known result. Neither is a defect-finding study; both files say to validate on own labelled data. |
| Single blind adjudicator versus panel | web-01 option 3 favours a blind, different-family adjudicator over debate; web-03 notes a single large judge is the setup PoLL argues against and recommends different-vendor judges, or at least two judges with reported agreement for offline scoring. Reconciling point: web-01's adjudicator makes a binary blocking decision, while web-03 advises against a required numeric per-finding calibrator; the two are compatible only if the adjudicator is binary and its true-negative rate is measured. |
| Verbalised confidence quality | Xiong 2024 (AUROC about 62.7%, overconfident), Tian 2023 (better calibrated than token probabilities) and Ferrer 2026 (best ECE 0.166 but AUC 0.668) disagree on whether it is "good". Common ground: top-skewed and weakly discriminative. Each uses 2023-2026 models; none tested the project's current model set. |
| Rubric as anchor | Rubric order bias (HIGH, extracted abstract) and a weak 2026 study (LOW) both say rubric text alone does not anchor; evidence gating is better supported. |
| Self-preference size | Panickssery (mechanism: recognition) versus the 2026 reanalysis (about 90% explained by uncertainty on hard items). Reconciled by recommending both blinding and a strong different-family judge. |
| Unverified or excluded | Verbosity figure from a June 2026 21-judge study (arXiv 2606.19544) attributed by a blog (https://digitortoise.com/mt-bench-explained) and the "always-A in 8 of 9 judges" figure were not confirmed against the primary paper and are excluded. The Apollo post date is unverified. |

#### 5.3.6 External-research options for who judges and calibration (from web-03 and web-01; options, not decisions)

| # | Option |
|---|---|
| 1 | Do not make a numeric per-finding calibrator a required role in the shared core; prefer reviewer agreement, the deterministic citation or evidence check and a binary blocking decision; keep the calibrator optional, disabled by default, logging raw outputs for later fitting. |
| 2 | If a calibrator or grader is kept: fresh context with the finding as external input; a different vendor, not only a different class; rubric option and criterion order permuted across a small number of runs; blinded input with opaque labels and no model, panel or combo names in schema or paths. |
| 3 | Treat the merge step as the fuser (reads all rationales, emits one decision); keep reflect's degrade rules (single-reviewer fallback, low convergence) as the fallback when diversity is missing. |
| 4 | Measure judge quality: a small fixed bias battery (swap order, pad length, rename author labels, rename files), blinded-versus-unblinded score differences in telemetry, E2 ground-truth packages as the labelled set; report the grader's true-negative rate on known-false blockers; compare the panel with its best single reviewer. |
| 5 | Keep a standing audit sample of findings the panel dropped or passed. |
| 6 | Re-derive any numeric threshold (such as the 0.82 or 0.85 values in the Reuse-Miss rule or the 0.80 convergence value) per model from logged data. |
| 7 | For an offline panel-scoring judge, use a different vendor from every reviewer in the scored panels, or at least two judges from different vendors with reported agreement. |
| 8 | Flag as open: validate on the project's own labelled data before treating any option as settled. |

### 5.4 Finding location and fingerprinting across revisions

Source file: `research/web-04-finding-fingerprinting.md` (Tavily). Codebase context recorded there from research/03 and research/10: v1 `findings.cluster` and v2 `cluster_v2` use transitive O(n^2) union-find over a prose-harvested reference regex (misses `T01.02`, pulls `P1` from `D-P1`); replay of v1 found 195 chained rows and 83 mega-rows (up to 19 members over 8 sections); v2 flags chains but does not split them, and its section component is always empty so equal refs on one file merge at any distance (D6); the quality figure (precision 21 of 25 = 0.84, n=25, on a 50-pair stratified sample; its recall is not a population recall) is AI-labelled, human labels pending; anchors over 200 characters are rejected (D1); consumers need a location union (anchor, path plus line plus in_diff, file:section, multi-file).

#### 5.4.1 Fingerprint design and alert matching across commits

| Finding | Source | Date | Relevance | Relationship to codebase |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SARIF separates producer-supplied partial identity (`partialFingerprints`, versioned hierarchical keys, compared on the greatest common version), consumer-computed identity (`fingerprints`, populated by the result management system) and a separate grouping id (`correlationGuid`). Appendix B: build identity from tool, rule id, target path and logical location, which is "more resilient" than line numbers; `logicalLocation.fullyQualifiedName` is "particularly convenient for fingerprinting". | https://docs.oasis-open.org/sarif/sarif/v2.1.0/sarif-v2.1.0.html (OASIS SARIF 2.1.0 Errata 01, 3.27.2-3.27.4, 3.27.16-17, Appendix B) `[E]` excerpts, official; corroboration https://boostsecurity.io/blog/sarif-cant-save-you-now `[S]` blog | Date not shown | HIGH | supports the citation-based location model with version pinning (research/03 summary) and extends it: identity should be a dictionary of named, versioned components. Our findings have no stable id other than the anchor quote or cited reference. contradicts v2's empty section, which discards the component the spec calls most change-resilient (extends the D6 diagnosis). |
| GitHub code scanning matches alerts across runs only through `partialFingerprints.primaryLocationLineHash` plus `ruleId` and a consistent path; inconsistent paths close the old alert and open a new one; results are also scoped by automation category. | https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/reference/code-scanning/sarif-files/sarif-support `[E]` official | Date not shown | HIGH | extends. Identity tuple (category, ruleId, path, location hash); path normalisation (repo-relative, forward slashes) is a prerequisite for PR in_diff findings and spec-anchor findings. Our v2 clusterer keys on path; add rule or category as a hard key. |
| When the line hash was empty (a finding with no line), GitHub matched alerts by their order in the file and fixing one finding closed another; supplying a per-result hash from rule, reason code and content fixed it. Single issue report. | https://github.com/SureA11y/core/issues/47 (issue, LOW to MEDIUM) | Oct 2026 | HIGH | supports. Direct analogue of the v2 empty-section over-merge (D6 family): a finding with no resolvable location needs a content-derived component, never an empty one. |
| GitHub shows an alert on a PR only if all its lines are inside the diff. | https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/code-scanning/code-scanning-alerts `[E]` official | Date not shown | MEDIUM | extends: `in_diff` is a display or placement filter, so keep it out of the cluster key (per-revision state, not identity). |
| CodeQL `primaryLocationLineHash`: a rolling hash of each line plus the next 100 non-space characters (whitespace skipped, line endings normalised), identical hashes in a file get a `:n` suffix; independent of line number and indentation, broken by an edit inside the window. | https://github.com/github/codeql-action/blob/main/src/fingerprints.ts `[E]` official source; https://github.com/aquasecurity/trivy/discussions/9070 (community reverse-engineering, MEDIUM) | Date not shown | HIGH | extends. Three ordered independent signals with a rule-equality gate and an explicit match reason that could be logged per cluster; rename handling maps to version pinning. v2 has no category gate in its key. |

| Code Climate engine spec: `fingerprint` is a unique deterministic identifier, default is a hash of the referenced code; occurrence-number suffixes keep duplicates distinct; otherwise GitLab shows only the last occurrence per fingerprint. | https://github.com/codeclimate/platform/blob/master/spec/analyzers/SPEC.md (official); https://github.com/troessner/reek/issues/1115 (issue, LOW to MEDIUM); https://aarongoldenthal.com/posts/gitlab-code-quality-duplication-analysis-with-pmd-cpd (blog, LOW to MEDIUM) | Dates not shown | MEDIUM | supports the occurrence-suffix idiom and a hazard: two occurrences sharing one fingerprint display as one, so a cluster with N members must list all member locations. |
